allOwnReferenceParagraphs.text: 2.1 We construct the smooth approximants rather than assume a distributional regularization theorem. By [F5] choose $b\ge0$ compactly supported and equal to one on a neighborhood of a closed box of positive volume inside the unit ball. Rescale its support into the unit ball. By [F6], $0<\int b<\infty$; put $\rho=b/\int b$ and $\rho_\epsilon(z)=\epsilon^{-n}\rho(z/\epsilon)$. For a compactly supported distribution $v$, define $v_\epsilon(y)=\langle v(z),\rho_\epsilon(y-z)|dz|\rangle$. It is smooth by [F4], supported in the $\epsilon$-neighborhood of $\operatorname{supp}v$, and has common compact support for $0<\epsilon\le\epsilon_0$. Pairing against a test $h$ and using [F4] gives $\langle v_\epsilon,h\rangle=\langle v,h_\epsilon\rangle$, where $h_\epsilon(z)=\int\rho(w)h(z+\epsilon w)dw$. Every derivative of $h_\epsilon-h$ tends uniformly to zero on the common compact support, by uniform continuity of the corresponding derivative of $h$. The finite-order bound proves weak convergence and a common order bound, because the averaging bounds every derivative seminorm of $h_\epsilon$ by the corresponding seminorm of $h$ on a fixed enlarged compact. The same interchange, or Fourier testing, gives $$\widehat{v_\epsilon}(\eta)=\widehat\rho(\epsilon\eta)\widehat v(\eta),\qquad |\widehat\rho(\epsilon\eta)|\le\int\rho=1.$$ Hence all polynomial and regular-cone bounds for $v$ are uniform in $\epsilon$. For a smaller local cutoff $a$, first choose $b_0=1$ near its support, inside a wavefront-regularity localization. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, $a(\rho_\epsilon*v)=a(\rho_\epsilon*(b_0v))$; step 1.1 gives the uniform regular-cone bound. The finitely many initial terms of a sequence $\epsilon_j\downarrow0$ are smooth and have their own finite rapid bounds. Compactness and finite subdivision into regular base/cone patches handle any compact cutoff/cone pair disjoint from $\operatorname{WF}(v)$. Thus these approximants are controlled on each smaller patch. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 Fix $x_0\in N$ and use one source chart and one target chart about $y_0=f(x_0)$, of positive dimensions for now. On their unit frequency spheres set $K_0=\{\eta:df_{x_0}^T\eta=0\}$. It is compact and disjoint from the compact fiber $\Gamma_{y_0}\cap S^{m-1}$. Choose an open conic neighborhood $V$ of $K_0$ with closure of directions still disjoint from that fiber. Closedness of $\Gamma$ implies that the same disjointness holds over a sufficiently small target neighborhood: otherwise points of $\Gamma$ approaching $y_0$, with directions in the compact closure, have a subsequence with a forbidden limit. Outside $V$, compactness gives $|df_{x_0}^T\eta|\ge2c|\eta|$; shrink the source chart so $|df_x^T\eta|\ge c|\eta|$ there. Shrink again so its image lies in the target neighborhood and choose its target cutoff $\beta$ supported there. If $K_0$ is empty take $V$ empty. Localized Fourier transforms $\widehat{\beta u}$ are rapidly decreasing on $V$: for each compact set of directions in $V$, the regularity witnesses over $\operatorname{supp}\beta$ give a finite base cover and cutoff decomposition; step 1.1 transfers the bounds, and a finite direction cover gives one bound for each order. Choose $V$ initially with closure inside this regular neighborhood, so the bounds hold on its whole set of directions. Only finitely many witnesses are used for each such estimate. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 On a compact source test support $H$ inside this small patch, choose $\beta=1$ near $f(H)$ and write $v=\beta u$. For $\omega=a(x)|dx|$ define $$T_a(\eta)=\int e^{2\pi i f(x)\cdot\eta}a(x)dx,\qquad P_f(v)(\omega)=\int\widehat v(\eta)T_a(\eta)d\eta.$$ On $V$, $\widehat v$ decreases arbitrarily fast and $|T_a|\le\operatorname{vol}(H)\sup|a|$. Off $V$, step 1.2 with $\xi=0$ gives $|T_a(\eta)|\le C_q(1+|\eta|)^{-q}p_q(a)$. Take $q>m+m_v+1$, where $m$ is the target dimension and $m_v$ is a finite-order exponent from [F2]. The integrals are absolutely convergent, with $|P_f(v)(\omega)|\le C p_q(a)$. This proves fixed-support continuity, hence a distribution by [F1]. If $v_j\to v$ is controlled, their common finite-order and regular-cone bounds give the same integrable majorant. Weak convergence gives $\widehat v_j(\eta)\to\widehat v(\eta)$ for each fixed $\eta$, so dominated convergence proves $P_f(v_j)(\omega)\to P_f(v)(\omega)$, with a uniform fixed-support order bound. For smooth $v$, Fourier inversion and absolutely integrable Fubini identify the value with $\int v(f(x))\omega(x)$. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 We prove the output cone estimate with uniform bounds, needed also for controlled limits. Fix an output direction $\xi_0$ at $x_0$ outside $f^*\Gamma$. Shrink the source base patch and its output cone $C$ about $\xi_0$. There is a target singular-direction cone $G$ containing every direction of $\Gamma$ over the target cutoff support such that for $\eta\in G$, $\xi\in C$ and $x$ in the source patch, $$|df_x^T\eta-\xi|\ge c_1(|\eta|+|\xi|).$$ To see this, normalize $|\eta|+|\xi|=1$. A sequence contradicting the bound has a convergent frequency subsequence and base limit. If the output frequency limit were zero, local transversality from step 2.2 forces the input frequency limit to be zero; if the input limit were zero the equation forces the output limit to be zero. Both contradict normalization. Otherwise the limit is a covector in $f^*\Gamma$ with output direction in the chosen excluded closed cone. Closedness and compactness therefore give the separation after shrinking; choose a slightly larger closed input cone still satisfying it. The complement of $G$ is regular for the localized input. To Fourier transform a compact output localization replace $a$ in step 3.1 by $a(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. On $G$, apply step 1.2 and the polynomial input bound. Its integral is at most $C_q(1+|\xi|)^{-q+m+m_v}$ after increasing $q$. Off $G$, use a uniform bound $B$ for $df_x^T$. For $|\eta|\le|\xi|/(2\max(1,B))$, the phase is nonstationary and the same estimate applies. For the remaining regular input frequencies, the bound on $T_a$ and arbitrary input decay give $C_N(1+|\xi|)^{-N+m}$ after integration. Taking these exponents arbitrarily large proves rapid output decay on $C$. The estimates use only common input bounds, so they hold uniformly for controlled sequences. The set $f^*\Gamma$ is closed locally away from the zero section: transversality bounds $|\eta|$ by a constant times $|df_x^T\eta|$ on $\Gamma$ over a smaller compact patch, allowing the same compactness argument. Thus the output weak limits and these uniform bounds give exactly the claimed controlled convergence. [F2, F3, F6, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra]

4.2 The formula is independent of the allowed target cutoff. For two cutoffs equal to one near $f(H)$, first work inside one of the small target neighborhoods of step 2.2. Their difference times $u$ is a compact distribution $w$ zero on a neighborhood of the compact set $f(H)$. Its mollifications from step 2.1 vanish at every $f(x)$, $x\in H$, for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, since their supports expand by at most $\epsilon$ and the two closed compact sets have positive Euclidean distance. Their ordinary smooth pullbacks therefore pair to zero with $\omega$. The controlled continuity in step 3.1 makes $P_f(w)(\omega)=0$. If the two originally allowed target neighborhoods differ, insert a third cutoff supported in their overlap and equal to one near the image of a smaller source support; compare with it in each neighborhood and use a finite decomposition of $\omega$. This also proves locality and independence of extensions outside the target chart. [F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Controlled convergence is invariant under a smooth change of coordinates. For completeness, the Fourier estimate is the one for a diffeomorphism, not an assumed arbitrary-map pullback. In source coordinates $y=\psi(z)$, the localized transformed Fourier value pairs $v_j$ with $a(\psi(z))|\det D\psi(z)|e^{-2\pi i\psi(z)\cdot\eta}$. Insert a cutoff equal to one on this compact support and use Fourier inversion [F4]. The resulting phase is $z\cdot\zeta-\psi(z)\cdot\eta$. In the near-stationary region $\zeta$ is comparable to $\eta$ and lies in a regular source cone whenever the transformed compact base/output cone avoids the transported $\Gamma$; there use the uniform regular bounds and a polynomial volume estimate. On the complementary region $|\zeta-D\psi(z)^T\eta|\ge c(|\zeta|+|\eta|)$; step 1.2 and the uniform polynomial bound give arbitrary rapid decay after integration. This is precisely the chart-invariance estimate with constants uniform in $j$. Common finite-order bounds transfer by the finite chain/product rules for compactly supported test densities, and weak convergence transfers because diffeomorphism pullback is already defined by the density transpose. Hence the same smooth approximants from step 2.1, expressed in either target chart, are controlled. Both local candidates in step 3.1 are their limits and equal the same ordinary smooth pullback at every stage. They are therefore equal. A change of source chart similarly gives the same smooth integrals by the absolute-Jacobian substitution in [F6], followed by the controlled limit. This proves coordinate covariance of the constructed scalar distribution and compatibility with the previously defined diffeomorphism pullback. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 We now glue; no assumption that $f(\operatorname{supp}\omega)$ fits one chart is made. Cover the compact support of a test density by finitely many small source patches of step 2.2. Shrink the covering patches still covering that support, take compact smooth cutoffs $b_i$ supported in the original patches and equal to one on the smaller ones, and put $s=\sum_i b_i$. It is positive near the test support. With another compact cutoff $h=1$ there and supported where $s>0$, set $a_i=hb_i/s$ there and zero elsewhere. They are smooth, subordinate, and sum to one near the test support. Define $\langle f^*u,\omega\rangle=\sum_i P_{f,i}(u)(a_i\omega)$. On an overlap the two terms are equal: shrink around each point to a common source patch and a target chart inside the two target-chart overlap, use step 4.2 for cutoffs and step 5.1 for coordinates, and decompose a compact overlap test into finitely many such patches. Two partitions now give the same answer by the double sum on $a_i a'_j\omega$. This proves linearity, independence and compatibility with restriction. For each fixed compact support choose this finite cover once. Each local pairing has a finite seminorm estimate by step 3.1; multiplication by the fixed $a_i$ is bounded by finitely many compact derivative seminorms. Their finite sum is continuous on that fixed-support space, and the test-density topology in [F1] gives a global distribution. Local estimates in step 4.1 give its wavefront bound and controlled sequential continuity. [F1, F5, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 If a source or target coordinate dimension is zero, every local distribution there is a scalar function, and the relevant local map is an ordinary smooth map from or to a point. For a zero-dimensional source, transversality forces the target distribution to be smooth near its image point, by [F3], so evaluation is defined; for a zero-dimensional target its local scalar pulls back as a constant. The finite-test gluing above handles zero-dimensional components, and an empty source has only the zero test space and its unique distribution. Zero inputs pull back to zero. Nonproper $f$ has required no extra hypothesis: each construction used only a compact source test support and its compact image. Finally any other rule agreeing on smooth inputs and obeying the stated controlled sequential continuity agrees on each small patch by the actual approximants of step 2.1, hence agrees globally by step 6.1. All coverings and comparisons for one test use finite choice only; [A1] enters exactly through the declared Fourier and Lebesgue suppliers. [A1, F1, F3, step 2.1, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

The local separation in step 2.2 precedes every Fourier construction. Transversality at points over $f(x)$ is not replaced by a single conic separation over the image of an arbitrary compact source set. Smooth approximation here has explicitly proved common finite-order and rapid-decay bounds; weak convergence alone would not justify a singular pullback limit.

2.1 For a compactly supported smooth test $h$, consider $$\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^s}\left(\prod_{j=1}^s\widehat v_j(\eta_j)\right)\widehat h\!\left(-\sum_j\eta_j\right)d\eta_1\cdots d\eta_s.$$ It is absolutely convergent. In the first region of step 1.1, use arbitrary rapid decay of the indicated comparable-size regular factor and polynomial bounds for the others; in the second, use arbitrary rapid decay of $\widehat h$. For every prescribed $Q$ both bounds are at most $C_Qp_{n_Q}(h)(1+R)^{-Q}$ after increasing the rapid exponent above $Q+\sum_jm_j$; the finite region $R\le1$ has the same bound with a larger constant. Choose $Q>sd$. Integration proves a finite-seminorm distribution estimate. For smooth compact factors the value is exactly $\int h\prod_jv_j$ by Fourier inversion and absolutely integrable Fubini. Approximate every $v_j$ by the controlled smooth sequences in [F3], with independent approximation indices. Their uniform bounds give the same integrable majorant. Each Fourier factor converges pointwise, so dominated convergence identifies every joint or iterated approximation limit with this one integral. This defines a simultaneous product and proves its invariance under reordering the factors. [A1, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The preceding bounds also give the common finite-order and regular-cone estimates for all intermediate products. To check the latter, replace $h$ by $h(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$. If an output cone avoids every nonzero sum of covectors from the selected $\Gamma_j\cup0$, compactness of normalized tuples implies that either a comparable-size factor is in a regular cone or $|\xi-\sum_j\eta_j|$ is comparable to $|\xi|+R$. Use rapid decay of that factor or of $\widehat h(\xi-\sum_j\eta_j)$ exactly as in step 2.1. Taking exponents arbitrarily large gives uniform rapid decay in that output cone. Noncancellation makes the cone sums locally closed away from zero: bounded output covectors bound the sum of the norms of input covectors, by step 1.1, and thus allow a convergent subsequence. Weak convergence on tests was already proved. Hence the intermediate products converge in the explicitly controlled sense of [F3]. For two factors this limit equals the product in [F4], because controlled tensor approximants and the diagonal pullback in [F3] have precisely that smooth limit. Group any subset first and repeat: its sum cone satisfies the next product condition whenever the full simultaneous condition holds. Controlled continuity and the common multi-frequency integral therefore prove every such iterated product agrees with the simultaneous one. These arguments are local; [F3], using the same transformed approximants and finite support partitions, makes the product cutoff- and coordinate-independent. [F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 We prove that the Statement's matching actually satisfies the simultaneous condition. Pull $a$, $b$ and each edge kernel to the full configuration space $M^{p+q}$ by their coordinate projections; these projections are submersions, so [F3] applies without a conormal restriction. The coefficient tensor has compact support. Insert edge cutoffs equal to one near the projections of that compact support; all later expressions then have one fixed compact support neighborhood. A possible zero-sum covector of these factors consists of a tuple $\alpha\in\operatorname{WF}(a)\cup0$ in block $A$, a tuple $\beta\in\operatorname{WF}(b)\cup0$ in block $B$, and, on each nonzero singular edge, a pair $(k,-\ell)$ with $k,\ell$ future null by [F2]. All smooth edges have zero wavefront covectors. Because the matching slots are disjoint, the zero-sum equations say that each $A$ entry is past null or zero, each $B$ entry is future null or zero, and every unused entry is zero. If any singular edge is nonzero, both full coefficient tuples are nonzero and forbidden by [F1]. If every singular edge is zero, disjointness of the two coefficient blocks forces $\alpha=\beta=0$ too. Thus there is no nonzero simultaneous zero sum. Closedness and compactness on each small product-chart patch give exactly the enlarged cones and estimates in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1. A compact coefficient support needs only finitely many such patches; no global cone over unrelated base points is assumed. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 All intermediate operations in an edge-contraction order are admissible, including those after earlier integrations. Every such intermediate kernel is the product of some of the original factors, pushed forward over some already matched variables, with the other original slots still labelled. Its possible wavefront covectors lift, by [F4], to sums of original factor covectors with zero entries in those previously integrated slots. If a later product had opposite covectors, insert that opposing factor and put zero in the other, as yet unused, factors. Lifting the zero vertical entries gives a nonzero simultaneous zero-sum tuple for a subset of the original factors, contradicting step 4.1 (a subset is included in the full condition by zero entries for the omitted factors). Thus the later product is transverse. The same argument applies when a smooth self-contraction in one coefficient has first been pushed forward and is then tensored with the other coefficient: the zero-covector obstruction lifts to the original coefficient block and its zero integrated entries. Product support stays inside the compact coefficient supports and their projections. Consequently each step has the controlled continuity from steps 3.1 and 1.2. Choose the common smooth approximants with the original slot structure preserved: regularize $a$ on its own $p$-slot block, $b$ on its own $q$-slot block, and each singular edge on its own two slots. Before lifting an edge, multiply by a pair-slot cutoff equal to one near the projection of one fixed compact neighborhood of the coefficient supports; leave every smooth edge unchanged. Pull these approximants back by the corresponding coordinate projections. These are submersions, so [F3] transfers controlled convergence; steps 3.1 and 1.2 give the same intrinsic product and pushforward limits. No arbitrary full-configuration smoothing or cutoff is introduced into a factor. At the smooth level the integrand is the product of the two original coefficient functions and the edge functions of their own labelled slots. A later edge has no dependence on slots removed by an earlier edge, because the edges form a matching; the as-yet unused other coefficient block likewise has no such slot. Thus precisely those later factors may be taken outside the earlier integration. Common compact coefficient supports make every relevant integrand integrable, and ordinary Fubini proves equality of the partial and simultaneous contractions. Taking the controlled limits proves equality with the canonical simultaneous product followed by pushforward, for every permitted edge order. This is a limit proof on the singular coefficient class, not an appeal to density of smooth coefficient kernels in the test-function topology. [F3, F4, F6, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 1.2, algebra]

6.1 The output is microcausal. Suppose a nonzero output wavefront covector were all future causal. Its lift before the final pushforward has these external entries and zero entries in every integrated slot. In the product wavefront sum from step 3.1, each singular edge then requires a past-null or zero coefficient entry in block $A$ and a future-null or zero coefficient entry in block $B$. Every other integrated coefficient entry is zero because its edge is smooth. Thus the full $B$ coefficient tuple, including its external entries, is all future. If any singular edge is nonzero it is a nonzero forbidden tuple. If all singular edges are zero, a nonzero output must instead come from a nonzero all-future tuple in at least one coefficient block, again forbidden. For an all-past output use block $A$ when a singular edge is nonzero and the identical no-edge argument otherwise. This proves exclusion of both cones, including cases where all external covectors of one block vanish. Compactness follows from the coefficient support and its projection, not from a global support assumption on $W$ or a smooth edge. [F1, F2, F4, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Relabeling slots is a diffeomorphism of the full configuration space. Smooth multiplication and integration commute with that relabeling, and the identical controlled-limit argument from [F3] and step 5.1 proves it for these distributions. For a polynomial functional, expand its finite coefficient expression before differentiation. A directional derivative selects one of the still uncontracted original slots and inserts its smooth direction there; the finite product rule assigns each labelled external direction to exactly one original coefficient block. Multiplication by these smooth directions and compact integration have the same controlled bounds, so the identity persists after every contraction. Symmetrizing remaining slots is a finite average of the proved permutation identity. For degree-zero coefficients there are no slots in that block and hence no incident singular edge; empty matchings give the original tensor and ordinary multiplication, and zero coefficients give zero. This proves all asserted derivative and permutation rules without a choice of representations or an infinite series limit. [F1, F3, F6, step 5.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 The singular edges in every coefficient of $D_W$ connect the two original functional blocks. Each application of a smooth $\Gamma_K$, including one applied after multiplication of the two functionals, pairs two remaining slots and hence gives either a smooth self-edge or a smooth cross edge of exactly the stated class. Every original slot is removed at most once. Steps 4.1 and 5.1 prove admissibility and equality of all those coefficient contractions, and step 7.1 supplies their finite Leibniz and permutation identities. Finite polynomial degree makes all sums at each coefficient finite, so these are precisely the compatibility rules needed for the finite Wick-change rearrangement. None of this treats a singular self-edge: such an edge would place opposite future/past entries in one coefficient tuple and would evade the contradiction in step 4.1. The distinction in the Statement is therefore essential. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

The simultaneous noncancellation condition in step 1.1 is proved for the actual matching in step 4.1, and every later use after a pushforward is checked again in step 5.1. No claim that arbitrary pairwise-defined distribution products may be regrouped is used. Smooth changes of a Hadamard kernel have exactly the self-contraction regularity required here.
